title: [Autour de La "Longue Marche" à travers la théorie de Galois, pages 1 à 67] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting. K is a field finitely generated over Q. U is a hyperbolic curve over K, X = Û is its smooth completion, and I is the set of cusps. Bars mean base change to the algebraic closure K̄ (so Ū = U⊗K̄, X̄ = X⊗K̄ and I = X̄ − Ū). Write π̄ = π₁(Ū), the geometric fundamental group. E_K = Gal(K̄/K), and E_U = π₁(U) is the arithmetic fundamental group, an extension of E_K by π̄. E_L is the analogous extension for the function field L, an extension of E_K by π_{L/K} (the birational or 'anabelian Galois' object of the previous page).

(1) First lines. These finish a statement begun on p.56: the 'model' form of the section conjecture (for U) reduces to the 'birational' form. One makes the latter precise by requiring that a section of E_U → E_K lift to a section of E_L → E_K. Equivalently, it should lift to a section of E_V → E_K for every open V ⊂ U. The section conjecture for U and for all its open subcurves is thus tied to the birational section conjecture.

(2) Geometric reformulation. Let Ũ be the pro-universal covering of U (a pro-scheme). Let X' be the normalization of X in Ũ, i.e. the limit of the complete smooth models of the finite covers. Grothendieck refuses to write X̃ because X' is not étale over X: it is ramified over the cusps.

For each cusp i ∈ I, the points of the fibre X'_i correspond bijectively to the inertia ('loop') subgroups of π̄ at i. Each such subgroup is the stabilizer of a point. Together they form one conjugacy class L_i.

Hence X' = Ũ ⊔ X'|I, where X'|I is the set of all loop subgroups of π̄. These are 'points at infinity' of the universal covering. On the next page E_U is read as the group of U-automorphisms of Ũ. A section E_K → E_U is then a continuous action of Γ = E_K on Ũ, compatible with its action on K̄.

This leads to Conjecture B: every such action has exactly one fixed point in X'. The fixed point is either a point of Ũ over a rational point (a geometric section) or a cusp (a cuspidal section, whose image lies in the normalizer of an inertia group).

The purpose is to put the section conjecture, including its cuspidal sections, into a fixed-point form on the compactified pro-universal cover.
errors: No real error. The 1-1 correspondence between points of X'_i and the loop subgroups at i is correct in characteristic 0 (tame inertia, procyclic Ẑ(1)), provided L_i is read as the set of inertia subgroups over i (a single conjugacy class), not as a set of conjugacy classes.

Degenerate non-hyperbolic case: for G_m (two cusps) both cusps have inertia equal to all of π̄. The bijection still holds cusp by cusp, but the 'unique fixed point' of Conjecture B fails. Grothendieck implicitly assumes 2g+ν ≥ 3, as stated on the previous page.
The phrase 'scindage de E_V → E_K, où V est un modèle ⊂ U' is a sketch. Lifting to every open V is equivalent to lifting to E_L only after a limit (compactness) argument, which is not given.

ideas.what: Sections of π₁(U) → G_K should lift to sections for every open V ⊂ U, equivalently to the birational Galois group (passing from the 'model' form to the 'birational' form of the section conjecture).
ideas.modern_name: Birational section conjecture; lifting of sections to neighbourhoods
ideas.usually_credited_to: Grothendieck (1983 letter to Faltings); developed by Koenigsmann, Pop, Esnault–Wittenberg, Stix
ideas.where_published: Letter to Faltings (1983) states the section conjecture, including the birational variant; the lifting formulation is discussed in Stix's book

ideas.what: Normalization X' of the complete curve in the pro-universal cover; cusps of X' correspond to inertia (loop) subgroups of π̄, i.e. 'points at infinity' of Ũ.
ideas.modern_name: Cuspidal inertia subgroups / compactified profinite universal cover
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard (SGA1 tame ramification theory; Nakamura, Tamagawa, Mochizuki on cuspidal decomposition groups)
ideas.where_published: SGA1 XIII (tame fundamental group, inertia at the boundary); implicitly in the Faltings letter

ideas.what: Section conjecture as a fixed-point statement: every continuous Γ-action on Ũ (a section) has exactly one fixed point in X', in Ũ (rational point) or at a cusp (cuspidal section).
ideas.modern_name: Section conjecture with cuspidal sections, fixed-point formulation
ideas.usually_credited_to: Grothendieck (letter to Faltings, 1983); fixed-point and neighbourhood viewpoint in Nakamura, Tamagawa, Stix's 'Rational points and arithmetic of fundamental groups'
ideas.where_published: Letter to Faltings (1983) mentions sections at infinity; this explicit fixed-point form appears in the Longue Marche notes

missed.claim: This is an early (pre-1983 letter) formulation of the section conjecture, including cuspidal sections, as a unique-fixed-point statement on the cusp-compactified pro-universal cover. Historically it predates the Faltings letter, but the mathematical content is now standard.
missed.quote: X'|I = ensemble des sous-groupes lacets de π̄, qui apparaissent ainsi comme des "points à l'infini" du revêtement universel Ũ
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mainly historical: it documents that the fixed-point / points-at-infinity viewpoint (later used by Tamagawa, Mochizuki and Stix) was Grothendieck's own framing from the start.

deep.surprise_reason: The fixed-point formulation with cusps as points at infinity of the universal cover is essentially the known modern framing of the (cuspidal) section conjecture. The page is a historically interesting early version, but not mathematically new.
transcription_corrections: 'sous forme modulaire' is probably 'sous forme modéliste' (cf. 'forme modéliste' on the previous page), i.e. the form in terms of models U.
'NB je n'ose pas de la noter X̃' is probably 'NB je n'ose pas le noter X̃'.
'les classes L_i des π̄' is probably 'les L_i des π̄', the set of loop subgroups at i; the interlinear insertion may read 'lacets' rather than 'classes'.
'par un un scindage' is likely 'par un un scindage' = '(ou aussi, pour un un scindage...)' with a duplicated word.
